title: The Mbuti of the Ituri Forest in Zaire

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For perhaps two millennia, the Ituri Forest of northern Zaire in Africa has been the home for both Mbuti hunter-gatherers and Bautu village-dwelling cultivators. The cultivators are settled in isolated villages using only small areas of the forest. The population density in the forest including both Mbuti and cultivators is low, averaging less than three persons per km2. More than 70% of the forest has probably never been cut and large areas remain uninhabited. Although never totally out of touch with villagers, Mbuti spend a great deal of time in the uncultivated parts of the forest. They are considered by all, including themselves, as the guardians of the forest, being the most familiar with the forest and the most efficient at extracting its resources. This alone, however, is not enough to assure Mbuti security. All Mbuti live as forest specialists in association with cultivators. Such interaction is key to their welfare and their future.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Economic aspects of the reciprocity between Mbuti and villagers have been described in some detail. Starch foods from villagers' gardens make up a significant part of Mbuti diet year-round. In turn, Mbuti provide villagers on an irregular basis with 'prestige foods', for example honey from the forest. They help clear and harvest the gardens and participate in seasonal fishing expeditions. Mbuti also provide diverse forest supplies, such as thatching and construction materials, firewood and medicinal plants. Trade relations between Mbuti and the villagers are not rigidly defined; there are no fixed terms. In most cases no cash is involved, and donations may even take the form of gifts. Mbuti, as monads, are highly unpredictable in what they will provide and when they will provide it. Villagers, on the other hand, have fairly predictable yearly cycle of activities centered on the preparation, planting and harvesting of their gardens.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Important elements in Mbuti-villager reciprocity extend beyond its economic base. For lack of a better term, these elements might be categorized as 'cultural reciprocity'. Under various circumstances, Mbuti use the more hierarchical and formalized social structure of villager societies. For example, in the southern and central Ituri Forest, villagers play a prominent role in Mbuti marriages and deaths, and in mediating outbreaks of conflict among Mbuti. Although Mbuti themselves will decide who will marry whom, and although they may not abide by the recommended terms in cases of arbitration, they nevertheless turn to villagers when wealth or formality is needed. Villagers often organize the resources needed for a wedding feast and delegate responsibilities at a funeral. Even if a death happens in a remote forest camp, the burial takes place in the village. Likewise, individuals involved in any crime occurring in the forest are brought by Mbuti to a village tribunal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: At other times, the villagers use Mbuti to act as intermediaries with the forest. Just as Mbuti use the more elaborate political structures of villagers to regulate certain aspects of their own social system, so villagers require the spiritual unity Mbuti have with the forest to assure their own relationship with the land. In the Harvest Festivals of cultivators of the southern Ituri, Mbuti even take precedence over village ritual authorities. At the start of the Harvest, the first crop bananas is for the ancestors and is left to rot on the plant. The second goes to Mbuti, and only the third for the mwami (king). Mbuti ease and independence in the forest is acknowledged to be a manifestation of their special relationship with the forest, a unity which the villagers cannot achieve in their more hierarchical, agriculturally-orientated lives. Mbuti participate at major ceremonies, including coronation ceremonies of the mwami, and the opening of new barazza (men's communal house).

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The exchange relationship between Mbuti and villagers has been flexible enough to survive a number of migrations and political upheavals in the past, and the Bantu are not the villagers to benefit from this relationship. Immigrants from north Africa entered the forest more than a century ago, and their descendants, the Baungwana, remain there today. The Baungwana are a Swahili-speaking agricultural group, who have not only established themselves in the forest, but have had Mbuti associated with their villages for at least three or four generations. These relatively recent relationships resemble the established Mbuti-Bantu interactions in many ways. The Baungwana come from a different cultural background, but in the Ituri Forest they are also small-scale, subsistence cultivators. Not only do they need forest products, but also, even more so than the indigenous forest Mbuti for their forest skills.
